text: In the last two lessons, a matrix moved every point of the plane and carried the grid lines along with it. Some transformations spread space out and others squeeze it together, so it would be useful to have a single number that says by how much. That number is called the determinant, and in this lesson we find out what it measures and why it matters.

Start with the unit square, the small tile that sits between the two basis arrows, i hat and j hat, with an area of exactly one. When a matrix acts, the tile is carried along with the grid: its sides become the two columns of the matrix, so the square turns into a parallelogram. Because grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced, every tile in the plane changes in the same way, which is why one number can describe the whole transformation.

Take the matrix with three and two on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. It stretches the horizontal direction by three and the vertical direction by two, so the unit tile becomes a rectangle of area six. Any shape you draw, however irregular, has its area multiplied by six as well, rather like a sheet of dough under a rolling pin, where every patch is stretched by the same factor.

A shear is a good test of intuition. It slides the top of the tile sideways while the bottom stays put, so the square leans over into a parallelogram that looks quite different. Yet its base and its height have not changed, so its area is still one, and the determinant of a shear is exactly one.

For a general two by two matrix with entries a, b, c and d, the area of the parallelogram works out to a times d, minus b times c. You can read the formula as a story: a times d is the area the diagonal entries would make on their own, and b times c is the correction for the columns leaning towards each other.

Now let the columns lean further, until they point along the same line. The parallelogram flattens into a thin sliver and then into a segment with no area at all, so the determinant is zero. The whole plane has been crushed onto a line, and that cannot be undone, because many different points have landed on the same spot. This is why a matrix with determinant zero has no inverse.

Keep pushing, and the determinant passes through zero and turns negative. The area is no longer shrinking; instead the tile has been flipped over, like a page turned face down, so that j hat now sits clockwise from i hat instead of anticlockwise. The sign of the determinant records this orientation, and its size records the stretch.

One last property ties this to composition. If you apply one matrix and then another, areas are scaled once and then scaled again, so the determinant of the product is the product of the determinants. In machine learning, a determinant near zero warns that a layer is crushing some direction flat and losing information, and later, when we fine tune language models with low rank updates, we will build such flattened matrices on purpose. Next, we return to the dot product and see it as a projection.
